html:
Three planes
Focus one equation
Click a coloured equation label in the figure (or a sheet itself): that plane stays solid, the others turn to glass, and an arrow along its normal shows the one coordinate it pins down.
Label check (optional)
As printed, the sheet is labelled y = −2 while the marked point reads (1, −1, 2). Tick the box to draw the red sheet at the y it is labelled with, and see the two disagree.
Label version

elements: Green plane x = 1: flat square sheet, normal along +x, standing upright and facing the viewer, drawn as a tilted parallelogram slightly left of center
Red plane y = -2: flat square sheet, normal along +y, perpendicular to the green sheet, reading as a tall diamond that passes behind and around the green sheet
Blue plane z = 2: flat square sheet, normal along +z, lying nearly horizontal and slicing through both other sheets at mid-height
Line where the green and red sheets cross (vertical line)
Line where the green and blue sheets cross (horizontal line running back-right)
Line where the red and blue sheets cross (horizontal line running right)
Small black dot near the center of the figure, on the green/blue crossing line
Thin black leader line from the dot up and to the right
Black text label '(1, -1, 2)' at the end of the leader line, upper right
Green text label 'x = 1' at the upper right edge of the green sheet
Red text label 'y = -2' centered below the figure
Blue text label 'z = 2' at the right edge of the blue sheet
Semi-transparent overlap shading so the visible wedges alternate in color where sheets cross

interactions.teaches: The three colored patches are not flat overlapping shapes but three mutually perpendicular infinite sheets; rotating shows they share exactly one point in space.

interactions.label: Add equations one at a time
interactions.teaches: One linear equation in three variables gives a plane, two give a line, and three give a single point — the solution set shrinks by one dimension per equation.
Clicking a sheet brightens it and dims the others, showing that each equation pins down exactly one coordinate while the other two stay free.

interactions.label: Red plane label
interactions.teaches: A point is a solution only if it lies on every plane at once: with the printed y = -2 the marked dot (1, -1, 2) sits one unit off the red sheet, and sliding the sheet to y = -1 makes all three equations true there.

demo_steps.title: One equation is a plane
demo_steps.narration: Only the green sheet is shown. Every point on it satisfies x = 1, with y and z completely free — one equation in three unknowns has a whole plane of solutions.

demo_steps.title: Two equations give a line
demo_steps.narration: Adding the blue sheet z = 2 leaves only the line where green and blue cross. Points on that line satisfy both equations at once.

demo_steps.title: Three equations give a point
demo_steps.narration: The red sheet cuts that line at a single point — the unique simultaneous solution of the three equations. Orbit to confirm the three sheets meet in exactly one place.

demo_steps.title: Check the marked point
demo_steps.narration: The printed dot is labeled (1, -1, 2), but the red sheet is labeled y = -2, so the dot floats one unit in front of the red sheet — it is not on all three planes.

demo_steps.title: Make the labels agree
demo_steps.narration: Sliding the red sheet to y = -1 brings it through the dot. Now (1, -1, 2) lies on all three planes, which is what it means to be the solution of the system.

plan.geometry_notes: Right-handed math orientation: x to screen-right-and-forward, y receding back-right, z up. Each plane is a square sheet 4 x 4 world units, drawn as a thin double-sided quad at ~0.78 opacity so crossings read as alternating colored wedges. Green plane x = 1: spans y in [-3, 1], z in [0, 4]; normal +x; appears upright, facing the viewer, positioned slightly left of center. Red plane y = -2 (or y = -1 in the consistent mode): spans x in [-1, 3], z in [0, 4]; normal +y; perpendicular to green, reads as a tall diamond passing behind and around the green sheet. Blue plane z = 2: spans x in [-1, 3], y in [-3, 1]; normal +z; nearly horizontal, slicing both others at mid-height. Black dot of radius ~0.07 drawn at (1, -1, 2) as printed — this sits exactly on the green/blue crossing line but one unit along +y off the printed red sheet; in the consistent mode the red sheet slides to y = -1 so the dot lies on all three. Leader line from the dot up-and-right ~1.8 units to the black text '(1, -1, 2)'. Label placement: green 'x = 1' at the upper-right edge of the green sheet; red 'y = -2' centered below the whole figure; blue 'z = 2' at the right edge of the blue sheet. Colors: green #22B14C, red #D62027, blue #1878A0, labels in matching colors, point label and leader line black; background white. No coordinate axes are drawn in this figure.
plan.notes: Build each sheet as a THREE.PlaneGeometry quad with MeshBasicMaterial, side: DoubleSide, transparent, opacity 0.78, depthWrite false, and render the three in back-to-front sorted order so the interlocking overlap reads correctly without z-fighting. Draw the three pairwise crossing lines as thin (1.5px) LineSegments in a darkened shade of the two crossing plane colors, with polygonOffset so they sit above the quads. Labels as CSS2DRenderer HTML overlays anchored to world positions so they stay screen-aligned and legible while orbiting. buildSolution simply fades planes in/out (300 ms) and shows the current solution set highlighted: whole green sheet, then the green/blue line as a thick line, then the single dot. planeFocus raises the clicked plane to opacity 1.0 and drops the other two to 0.22. labelCheck animates the red sheet sliding along y between -2 and -1 over ~500 ms, with a short dashed black connector from the dot to the red sheet visible only in the 'as printed' state so the one-unit gap is obvious. Limit orbit elevation so the camera does not flip below the blue sheet.

authoredPrompt: This figure shows three mutually perpendicular planes cutting through one another, drawn as flat colored parallelograms with no coordinate axes displayed. A green plane stands roughly upright facing the viewer, labeled x = 1 in matching green at its upper right. A red plane meets it at a right angle, tilted so it reads as a tall diamond passing behind and around the green sheet, labeled y = -2 in red beneath the drawing. A blue plane lies nearly horizontal and slices through both others, labeled z = 2 in blue at its right edge. The sheets overlap so each is partly hidden by the others, giving a sectioned, interlocking block in which the visible pieces alternate in color where they cross. A small black dot near the center is labeled (1, -1, 2), which conflicts with the red plane label y = -2; as drawn, the displayed point does not satisfy all three displayed plane equations. The drawing still gives geometric meaning to a system of three linear equations in three variables, but the plane label or point label must be corrected before the marked point can be treated as the simultaneous solution.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle individual planes on and off: the learner shows x = 1, y = -2, and z = 2 one at a time or together, while a warning highlights that the displayed point label (1, -1, 2) does not satisfy the red plane y = -2.
- Click for a plane label: the learner clicks a colored equation and its plane plus the coordinate it fixes are highlighted, making clear how each equation restricts one coordinate while leaving a full sheet of possible points.
- Toggle corrected-label overlay: the learner switches between the figure as printed and a corrected version, either y = -1 with point (1, -1, 2) or y = -2 with point (1, -2, 2), making clear that a solution must satisfy every plane equation simultaneously.
authoredContext:
The solution is the ordered triple (1,−1,2). See the figure.

An illustration of three orthogonal planes, x=1 (green), y=-2 (red), and z=2 (blue), intersecting at the labeled point (1, -1, 2) in a 3D coordinate system.

interactions.teaches: Each equation is a full flat sheet of points, and the three sheets are mutually perpendicular — rotating shows their single shared point rather than a flat overlap of colored patches.
Clicking a colored equation label highlights its sheet and the one coordinate it pins down, showing that each equation fixes exactly one coordinate and leaves the other two free.

demo_steps.title: One equation, one sheet
demo_steps.narration: Only the green plane x = 1 is shown: every point on this whole sheet satisfies x = 1, with y and z completely free.

demo_steps.title: Two equations, one line
demo_steps.narration: Adding the blue plane z = 2 leaves only the line where the two sheets meet — points satisfying both equations at once.

demo_steps.title: Three equations, one point
demo_steps.narration: The red sheet y = -2 cuts that line at a single point. This is the figure as printed — but the black dot is labeled (1, -1, 2), and -1 is not -2, so the marked point is not on the red sheet.

demo_steps.title: Fix the plane label
demo_steps.narration: Relabel the red sheet y = -1 and it now passes through (1, -1, 2): all three equations are satisfied at the marked point.

demo_steps.title: Or fix the point label
demo_steps.narration: Alternatively keep y = -2 and move the marked point to (1, -2, 2). Either way, a solution must lie on every plane simultaneously.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World space uses x right-ish, y receding, z up (standard math orientation). Each plane is a square sheet 4 x 4 world units, centered on the common intersection point, drawn as a thin double-sided quad with ~0.75 opacity so overlaps read as alternating wedges. Green plane: x = 1, spans y in [-3, 1], z in [0, 4] — normal +x, appears upright and roughly facing the viewer. Red plane: y = -2 (or y = -1 in corrected mode), spans x in [-1, 3], z in [0, 4] — normal +y, perpendicular to green, reads as a tall diamond behind/around it. Blue plane: z = 2, spans x in [-1, 3], y in [-3, 1] — normal +z, nearly horizontal, slicing through both. Intersection point of the three as printed would be (1, -2, 2); the black dot is drawn at the labeled (1, -1, 2), i.e. one unit off the red sheet along +y in 'As printed' mode, sitting exactly at the green/blue intersection line. Dot radius ~0.06 units, black. Leader line from dot up and to the right ~1.8 units to the '(1, -1, 2)' text. Colors: green #22B14C, red #D62027, blue #1878A0; label text in matching color, point label black. Label placement: 'x = 1' green at upper right of green sheet; 'y = -2' red centered below the figure; 'z = 2' blue at the right edge of the blue sheet; point label top right. Intersection lines drawn as 1.5px lines in a darker shade of the two crossing plane colors.
interactionPlan.notes: Use THREE.PlaneGeometry quads with MeshBasicMaterial, side: DoubleSide, transparent, opacity 0.78, depthWrite false and sorted rendering so the interlocking overlap reads correctly without z-fighting; add a slight polygonOffset on intersection lines. Labels as CSS2DRenderer/HTML overlays anchored to world positions so text stays screen-aligned and crisp while orbiting. Clicking a label (planeFocus) raises that plane's opacity to 1.0, dims the other two to 0.25, and draws a highlighted axis arrow along that plane's normal with the fixed coordinate value annotated. In 'As printed' mode render a small amber warning badge near the dot ('point not on y = -2') and draw a dashed 1-unit connector from the dot perpendicular to the red plane to make the mismatch visible. labelVersion transitions should animate the red plane sliding along y or the dot sliding along y over ~500 ms so the learner sees which object moved. Camera at standard isometric pose, orbit limited to avoid flipping below the blue plane's horizon.

discrepancies: In the source the black dot sits exactly at the triple intersection of the three sheets; the default ('as printed') state here offsets the red sheet one unit from the dot, so the dot floats off the red plane and an amber 'point not on y = −2' badge plus dashed connector appear on the canvas — neither exists in the source (the geometrically matching state is hidden behind the 'Corrected: point (1, −2, 2)' radio).

The '(1, −1, 2)' callout is placed just above the intersection and overlaps the sheets; in the source it sits well outside the figure at the top with a long thin leader line, giving a much cleaner annotation.
The dot itself and the leader line are very faint/thin in the render — in the source the dot is a clearly visible solid point anchoring the whole figure.

Plane extents/outlines differ slightly: the source shows three equal squares whose outlines read as clean overlapping diamonds; here the green and red sheets read as a slightly narrower star-like overlap, and the interior intersection lines are barely visible compared with the crisp edges in the source.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-coloured axonometric reconstruction of the three coordinate-parallel planes with excellent, pedagogically apt interactions (visibility toggles, plane focus with normal arrows, and a 5-step guided demo), slightly undermined by the default state deliberately displacing the red sheet from the labelled point and adding an on-canvas warning badge/dashed connector that are not in the source.

feedback.rationale: The main failure is a hallucinated 'as printed vs corrected point' narrative baked into the interaction design — the default state and warning badge/dashed connector contradict the source — which is a planning-level decision about what elements and states to include, not just a rendering slip.

discrepancies: Label collision: the green 'x = 1' label sits directly on top of the point label at the top of the figure, rendering as 'x =(1, −1, 2)' so the '1' of x = 1 is obscured; in the source the two annotations are clearly separated (point label top-centre with a long leader, x = 1 to the upper right of the green sheet).

Camera/axonometry differs: the generated view is nearly symmetric (both horizontal axes at 24°), so the vertical green and red sheets read as upright rectangles with slight slant, whereas the source uses a more oblique, asymmetric axonometric where each sheet reads as a clear rhombus/parallelogram and the blue sheet spreads much wider across the frame.

Sheet extents/proportions: in the source the three squares have visibly different apparent sizes and offsets (blue extends far to the left, red is largest and hangs low), while all three generated sheets are identical 4×4 squares centred on the point, producing a more uniform pinwheel than the printed figure.

Leader line direction: source leader runs from the dot up-and-slightly-right to a label above the green sheet's top edge; the generated leader angles steeply to the upper-right and terminates where it clashes with the x = 1 label.
Extra pedagogical UI text (label-check/mismatch narrative, relabel radio buttons) introduces content not present in the printed figure, though it is kept off the canvas by default.
evaluation.notes: Correct three-plane axonometric composition with proper mutual interpenetration, matching colours and a rich, conceptually-sound set of interactions (build-up demo, focus/normal arrows, intersection lines, label-consistency check); main weaknesses are the 'x = 1' label colliding with the point label and a more symmetric, uniformly-sized plane arrangement than the printed figure.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual decomposition and interactions are correct; remaining issues are implementation details (label collision, leader line placement, camera obliquity, sheet extents) best handled by refining the rendering.

discrepancies: Camera elevation is far too low: the blue z = 2 sheet is squashed into a thin sliver, whereas in the source it reads as a broad horizontal parallelogram roughly as prominent as the other two sheets.

The green x = 1 sheet is smaller and much more front-facing than in the source, where it is a strongly sheared parallelogram sweeping from lower-left to upper-right; the resulting pinwheel composition is flatter and less balanced.
Relative sheet proportions differ: the red y-sheet dominates the frame while in the source the three rectangles are more comparable in apparent area and interleave more visibly.

The red sheet is drawn at y = −1 by default (so it contains the marked point) while carrying the printed y = −2 label; correct pedagogically but the default view no longer matches the printed geometry-to-label pairing without reading the side panel.
The leader line to (1, −1, 2) starts at the dot and runs steeply up-left; in the source it is a shorter, straighter tick to the upper-right corner label — minor placement difference.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-labelled three-plane figure with genuinely rich and pedagogically apt interactions (per-plane toggles, focus highlighting, intersection lines, 5-step guided demo, and a thoughtful treatment of the source's label/point inconsistency); the main weakness is the too-low camera that flattens the blue z = 2 sheet into a sliver and loses the balanced pinwheel composition of the original.

feedback.rationale: The concept, plane set, labels, and interactions are all correct; the remaining issues are execution details (camera elevation, sheet extents/proportions, leader-line placement) that only need rendering adjustments.
